title: Is Spicy Food Good for a Hangover? Why It Often Backfires
excerpt: Is spicy food good for a hangover? What capsaicin does to a stomach alcohol has already irritated, when spicy soup is fine, when to skip the heat, and what helps instead.
metaDescription: Is spicy food good for a hangover? How capsaicin affects a stomach alcohol already irritated, when spicy soup is fine, and what to eat instead.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** spicy food doesn't cure a hangover, and for a lot of people it makes the worst part of one, the sore, acidic stomach, feel worse. Chili heat can give you a short-lived jolt of alertness and clear a stuffy nose, which is probably why so many cultures swear by a fiery morning-after soup. But alcohol has already irritated your stomach lining and loosened the valve that keeps acid out of your throat, and capsaicin (the compound that makes peppers hot) lands right on top of that. If your stomach feels fine and you love spicy food, a moderately spiced, salty, carb-rich meal with plenty of fluid is unlikely to hurt you. If you have heartburn, nausea, stomach pain, or diarrhea, save the hot sauce for another day.

> **When to see a doctor.** Most hangover stomach trouble clears within a day. Get medical help right away if you **vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds**, have **black or tarry stools**, have **severe belly pain**, especially pain that bores through to your back, **can't keep any fluids down** for many hours, or notice signs of serious dehydration such as dizziness when standing, very little urine, or confusion. **Chest pain, trouble breathing, or fainting means calling 911**, not waiting it out with an antacid. And if someone is very hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, or having a seizure after drinking, that's a possible alcohol poisoning emergency: call 911.

## Why People Reach for Spicy Food When Hungover

The idea that heat "burns off" a hangover is old and widespread. Some of the best-known hangover dishes in the world are spicy:

- **Menudo** in Mexico, a tripe soup in a red chile broth, is a classic weekend-morning hangover meal.
- **Haejang-guk** in Korea literally translates to "soup to chase a hangover." Many versions are mild beef or pork bone broths, but some are spiked with chili.
- **The Bloody Mary** and its cousin the Michelada lean on hot sauce, black pepper, and horseradish.
- **Pho with sriracha and chili**, hot-and-sour soups, and spicy ramen show up again and again in "what I eat when hungover" threads.

Notice what most of these have in common besides chili: they're **hot, salty, watery soups or drinks with some protein and carbs.** That combination genuinely helps a hungover body. You get fluid, sodium, and food to bring your blood sugar back up. The chili is the flavor people remember, but it's probably the least useful ingredient in the bowl.

People also describe a real sensation. Spicy food makes you sweat, makes your nose run, and gives you a jolt that feels like waking up. When you feel foggy and congested, that can be welcome. The question is whether that jolt is worth what capsaicin does to a stomach that's already irritated.

## What Capsaicin Actually Does in Your Body

Capsaicin doesn't burn anything. It binds to a receptor called **TRPV1**, which is the same sensor nerves use to detect real heat. Your brain gets a "this is hot" signal, and your body responds as if you were overheating: you flush, sweat, and your nose and eyes run.

That reaction explains most of what people feel after a spicy hangover meal:

- **A brief alertness boost.** Strong sensory stimulation of any kind, a cold shower, a loud noise, a mouthful of chili, wakes you up for a little while. Some researchers have suggested that the pain of capsaicin also triggers the body's own endorphins, which could add a mild feel-good effect, but this isn't something that has been measured in hungover people.
- **A clearer nose.** Spicy food commonly triggers a runny nose (doctors call it gustatory rhinitis). If you're congested after drinking, that can feel like relief, though it's temporary.
- **Sweating.** This is where the folk logic goes wrong. Sweating doesn't flush out alcohol or toxins in any meaningful amount. Your liver handles the vast majority of alcohol; only a small fraction leaves through breath, urine, and sweat. Sweating mainly costs you fluid you're already short on.

TRPV1 receptors aren't just in your mouth. They're found along the whole digestive tract, which is why a very spicy meal can make your stomach burn and speed things through your gut, sometimes all the way to an uncomfortable exit the next morning.

## The Problem: Alcohol Has Already Irritated Your Stomach

To understand why spicy food often backfires the morning after, it helps to know what drinking has done to your digestive system overnight.

### Alcohol inflames the stomach lining

Alcohol irritates the stomach lining directly and increases acid production. After a heavy night this can cause **acute gastritis**, meaning short-term inflammation of the stomach lining. It's a big part of why hangovers come with nausea, a gnawing ache in the upper belly, and loss of appetite. Our guide to [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) covers this in more detail.

### Alcohol relaxes the acid valve

There's a ring of muscle at the bottom of your esophagus that keeps stomach acid where it belongs. Alcohol relaxes it, which lets acid splash upward and causes heartburn and a sour taste. If you already get reflux, drinking makes it more likely. See our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) for why it happens and what helps.

### Alcohol speeds up your gut

Alcohol can irritate the intestines and rush food and fluid through them before water is properly absorbed. That's the cause of the infamous morning-after loose stool, covered in our article on [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking).

### Where capsaicin fits in

Now add a plate of hot wings or a bowl of chili-oil ramen:

- **Heartburn:** spicy food is one of the most commonly reported heartburn triggers. Not everyone reacts, but if you're prone to reflux, the combination of a relaxed valve and spicy food is a reliable way to feel worse.
- **Stomach burning and nausea:** capsaicin activates pain sensors in a stomach lining that's already inflamed. Many people with gastritis or indigestion find spicy food makes their symptoms worse, even if it isn't causing new damage.
- **Diarrhea:** capsaicin speeds gut movement too. Stacked on top of alcohol's effect, that can turn a mildly unsettled gut into an urgent one, with the bonus burn on the way out.

### Does spicy food actually damage your stomach?

This is worth being precise about, because the internet often overstates it. Research has generally **not** found that chili causes stomach ulcers in healthy people, and some lab and animal studies even suggest capsaicin can have protective effects on the stomach lining. So a spicy meal the morning after is unlikely to cause real harm in a healthy person.

The issue is **symptoms, not injury.** When your stomach is already inflamed and full of acid, capsaicin makes the burning, nausea, and urgency feel worse. When you're hungover, feeling worse is the whole problem you're trying to solve.

## Is Spicy Food Good for a Hangover? It Depends on Your Stomach

Here's a practical way to decide.

**Spicy food is probably fine if:**
- Your hangover is mostly a headache, tiredness, and fogginess, with a stomach that feels normal or hungry.
- You eat spicy food regularly and your gut is used to it.
- It's part of a real meal with carbs, protein, salt, and plenty of liquid, like a spiced noodle soup.
- You keep the heat moderate instead of chasing the hottest thing on the menu.

**Skip it or keep it mild if:**
- You have heartburn, a sour taste in your mouth, or a burning feeling in your chest or upper belly.
- You're nauseous or have already vomited.
- You have diarrhea or cramping.
- You have reflux disease, gastritis, IBS, or a history of ulcers.
- You don't normally eat spicy food. A hangover is a bad time to test your tolerance.

If you're not sure, start bland and add heat later. You can always put sriracha on a second bowl. You can't take it back out of your stomach.

## The Spicy Hangover Foods People Ask About

### Spicy soup and noodles

This is the best version of the spicy hangover meal, because the soup is doing most of the work. A big bowl of broth gives you fluid and sodium, which helps replace what alcohol pushed out through extra urination. Noodles or rice bring your blood sugar back up. Meat, tofu, or egg adds protein. If your stomach can handle the heat, a moderately spicy pho, ramen, menudo, or haejang-guk is a reasonable choice. If it can't, order the same soup mild and you keep nearly all the benefit.

### Hot wings, curry, and spicy fast food

These are the riskier picks. They tend to combine a lot of heat with a lot of fat, and fatty meals slow stomach emptying and can worsen reflux. A greasy, fiery meal on an irritated stomach is the most likely combination to leave you with heartburn and a dash to the bathroom. Our article on [greasy food and hangovers](/never-hungover/greasy-food-hangover) explains why fat is more helpful *before* drinking than the morning after.

### Hot sauce in a Bloody Mary

A Bloody Mary is really two separate hangover ideas. Tomato juice brings fluid, salt, and a little sugar. The vodka is "hair of the dog," which doesn't treat a hangover; it just postpones it, and it adds more alcohol to a stomach and liver that are still recovering. A **Virgin Mary** with a splash of hot sauce keeps the parts that might help and drops the part that definitely doesn't. Go easy on the heat if your stomach is sour.

### Spicy chips and snacks

Chips give you salt and carbs, which isn't nothing, but very spicy dusted snacks are a concentrated hit of capsaicin with little else. If that's all you have, eat a few with water and something plainer alongside.

### Chili peppers and capsaicin supplements

There's no good evidence that eating raw chilies or taking capsaicin capsules helps with a hangover, and capsaicin supplements can cause stomach upset on their own. This is one to skip.

## Does Spicy Food Before Drinking Help?

Some people eat a big spicy meal before going out, hoping it will "line the stomach." Any real meal before drinking helps, because food slows how fast alcohol moves from your stomach into your bloodstream. That benefit comes from the food itself, especially protein, fat, and fiber, not from the chili. There is no good evidence that spice adds anything to the protective effect.

There's a downside to consider too. A very spicy meal followed by a night of drinking stacks two acid-and-reflux triggers. If you're heartburn-prone, a moderately seasoned meal is the smarter base. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) covers what works best.

## Does Spicy Food While Drinking Make You Drink More?

It can. Spicy food makes you thirsty, and when the nearest drink is a beer, it's easy to drink faster than you planned. Bar snacks are often salty and spicy for that exact reason. If you're eating spicy food on a night out, keep a glass of water on the table and use it to put out the fire instead of your drink.

## What Actually Helps a Hangover Stomach

If spicy food isn't the fix, what is? None of these will make a hangover vanish, but they address the real causes of feeling rough.

1. **Rehydrate slowly and steadily.** Alcohol makes you urinate more. Sip water, or an electrolyte drink if you've been sweating, vomiting, or had diarrhea. Gulping a large amount on a queasy stomach can bring it back up, so small, frequent sips work better.
2. **Eat bland carbs first.** Toast, crackers, rice, bananas, oatmeal, or plain noodles bring your blood sugar back up without irritating your stomach. Once those stay down, add protein such as eggs.
3. **Try broth.** A plain or lightly seasoned soup gives you fluid, salt, and something warm. It's the useful core of every hangover soup, minus the chili.
4. **Ginger for nausea.** Ginger has reasonable evidence for some types of nausea, and ginger tea is gentle on the stomach. See our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) for more options.
5. **Be careful with painkillers.** Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can further irritate an inflamed stomach, so take them with food if you use them. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is easier on the stomach but harder on the liver after drinking, so read our guide on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) first.
6. **Rest.** Alcohol disrupts sleep quality, and a lot of hangover misery is plain sleep debt.

For a fuller list of foods ranked by what they do, see our guide to the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover).

## When Spicy Food After Drinking Signals Something More Serious

A spicy meal that leaves you with heartburn or a quick trip to the bathroom is unpleasant but normal. Some symptoms are not normal, and you shouldn't blame them on the chili:

- **Vomiting blood**, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds. Forceful vomiting after heavy drinking can tear the lining of the esophagus, and gastritis can bleed. Get urgent care.
- **Black, tarry stools**, which can mean bleeding higher up in the digestive tract. Note that red stool after a lot of red chili sauce or beets can be food coloring, but if you're unsure, get it checked.
- **Severe upper belly pain that spreads to your back**, especially with vomiting. Heavy drinking is a leading cause of pancreatitis, which needs medical care.
- **Chest pain or pressure.** Heartburn and heart problems can feel alike. If you have chest pain with shortness of breath, sweating, or pain spreading to your arm or jaw, call 911 rather than assuming it's reflux.
- **Heartburn several times a week**, whether or not you've been drinking. That's worth talking to a doctor about, since ongoing reflux can be treated and shouldn't be ignored.

If you notice that you regularly need a remedy for your stomach after drinking, it's also worth taking an honest look at how much and how fast you're drinking. The single most reliable way to avoid a hangover stomach is fewer drinks, spaced out, with food and water. Our guide to [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through the habits with the best evidence.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people add a supplement to their routine on nights they drink. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of that research is in animals and lab settings, with limited human data, so it's best described as promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that DHM settles an upset stomach, prevents heartburn, or protects against gastritis, and it won't change how your gut reacts to a plate of hot wings.

If you want to try it as part of a sensible drinking plan, alongside food, water, and pacing, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

Spicy food isn't a hangover cure. The famous spicy hangover soups work mostly because they're hot, salty, watery, and filling, not because of the chili. Capsaicin can give you a brief wake-up jolt and clear your nose, but it also tends to worsen the heartburn, stomach burning, and diarrhea that alcohol already causes. If your stomach feels fine, a moderately spicy soup with noodles and protein is a reasonable meal. If your stomach is sour, nauseous, or rushing, go bland first, drink fluids steadily, and add the heat another day.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is spicy food good for a hangover?**

Not really. Spicy food can make you feel briefly more alert and clear a stuffy nose, but it doesn't treat the causes of a hangover, and it often makes heartburn, stomach burning, and diarrhea worse. Spicy soups help mainly because of the fluid, salt, and carbs they contain. If your stomach feels fine, mild to moderate heat is unlikely to hurt.

**Why do I crave spicy food when I'm hungover?**

Hangovers often bring cravings for salty, intense, high-calorie food, partly because your blood sugar may be low and you've lost fluid and salt. Spicy food also delivers a strong sensory jolt that can feel like it cuts through the fog. The craving is real, but it's mostly your body asking for food, salt, and fluid, which a milder meal can also provide.

**Can spicy food make a hangover worse?**

Yes, for many people. Alcohol inflames the stomach lining, increases acid, relaxes the valve that keeps acid out of your esophagus, and speeds up your gut. Capsaicin can add to all of those symptoms, leading to more heartburn, burning, nausea, and diarrhea. People with reflux, gastritis, or IBS are most likely to notice it.

**Does spicy food help you sweat out alcohol?**

No. Your liver breaks down the vast majority of the alcohol you drink, and only a small amount leaves your body through sweat, breath, and urine. Sweating more from spicy food won't speed that up in any meaningful way. It just costs you fluid when you're already dehydrated.

**Is a Bloody Mary with hot sauce a good hangover cure?**

The tomato juice and salt can help a little with fluids, but the vodka just adds more alcohol and delays the hangover rather than fixing it. A Virgin Mary with a small amount of hot sauce is a better choice, and if your stomach is sour, skip the heat.

**Is spicy soup like menudo or pho good for a hangover?**

It can be a good choice if your stomach can handle it, mostly because of the broth, salt, protein, and noodles or hominy, not the chili. Order it mild or add heat gradually if your stomach feels irritated.

**Can I eat spicy food before drinking to prevent a hangover?**

Eating a real meal before drinking helps because food slows how quickly alcohol is absorbed. There's no good evidence that spice adds any extra protection, and a very spicy meal plus alcohol stacks two common heartburn triggers. A balanced meal with protein, carbs, and some fat is the better pre-drinking choice.

**When should I worry about stomach pain after drinking and spicy food?**

See a doctor urgently if you vomit blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, have black tarry stools, have severe belly pain spreading to your back, or can't keep fluids down for many hours. Call 911 for chest pain with shortness of breath or sweating, or if someone is hard to wake after drinking.
